Rinse burette with titrant and pipette with analyte; remove air bubble from burette tip; read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level; swirl; add dropwise near the end point.

front: Should the conical flask be rinsed with the analyte solution?
back: No — rinse it with distilled water only. Extra analyte would increase the amount present; water does not change the moles pipetted.
Finds the approximate end point quickly so accurate titres can be done dropwise near that volume; it is not included in the mean.

front: How to read a burette or pipette?
back: Eye level with the bottom of the meniscus (avoids parallax); burette to ±0.05 cm³ (2 d.p.).
Separates immiscible liquids: shake, vent, allow layers to settle, run off the lower (denser) layer through the tap.
Add an anhydrous salt (MgSO₄, Na₂SO₄ or CaCl₂) until it no longer clumps, then decant or filter.
Gas syringe, or displacement of water into an inverted measuring cylinder/burette (not for very soluble gases like NH₃, HCl).
Ensures the reaction/dehydration is complete (all water/volatile product removed) — repeat heating and weighing until mass stops changing.
Spot sample on a pencil baseline above solvent level; develop in a covered tank; mark solvent front; visualise (UV/iodine); calculate Rf.

front: Why draw the chromatography baseline in pencil and above the solvent?
back: Ink would dissolve and run; spots below the solvent would dissolve into the tank instead of moving up.
Choose a filter of the complementary colour; measure absorbance of standards; plot calibration curve; read unknown’s concentration from its absorbance.

front: Safety for volatile, flammable organic liquids?
back: Use a fume hood, no naked flames (heat with water bath or heating mantle), wear goggles and gloves.

front: Setting up a voltaic cell measurement?
back: Clean metal electrodes with sandpaper, use 1.0 mol dm⁻³ solutions, a salt bridge of filter paper soaked in KNO₃(aq), and a high-resistance voltmeter.
Calibrate with buffer solutions of known pH, rinse the probe with distilled water between readings, and keep temperature constant.

front: Why use anti-bumping granules and a water condenser in reflux?
back: Granules give smooth boiling; the condenser returns volatile reactants and products to the flask so nothing escapes and reaction can go to completion.
